gloss: roar, be in tumult; a tumult, a multitude
summary: To make a deep, continuous noise: the sea and its waves roar, a city is in commotion, a dog growls, doves moan, and the heart or inward parts of someone troubled or moved with pity do the same. Its noun הָמוֹן is that sound, then the tumult of many people, then the multitude itself, usually an army or a people in its numbers, and so abundance of anything; Abraham is named “father of a multitude of nations”. Scripture sets the roaring sea and the roaring nations side by side, and says that Yahweh stills both. The pronoun הֵמָּה, “they”, is spelled with the same letters but is the plural of הוּא and is treated there.

words.gloss: roar, growl, moan; be in commotion; be stirred within
words.summary: Only in the qal, 34 times, and nearly all in the prophets, Psalms and Proverbs. Its subject is whatever makes a deep, unbroken sound: the sea and its waves, an army, a city, a dog, bears, doves, a harp, flutes; and then the heart, soul and inward parts of someone troubled or moved.

stems.gloss: roar; growl, moan; be noisy, in commotion; be disquieted; be stirred with feeling

senses.definition: To make the deep, continuous sound of the sea: said of waves and waters, and of armies and nations whose voice is likened to them.

evidence.note: “Woe to the הֲמוֹן of many peoples: כַּהֲמוֹת יַמִּים יֶהֱמָיוּן, like the roaring of seas they roar”: the verb twice and its noun, with שָׁאוֹן and “mighty waters” beside them.
“וְהָמוּ גַלָּיו, its waves roar, and do not pass over” the sand Yahweh set as the sea's bound.
Of the army from the north: “their voice roars like the sea (קוֹלָם כַּיָּם יֶהֱמֶה)”; the same words of Babylon's foe in Jer 50:42.
Yahweh “stirs the sea, and its waves roar”; the same line in Jer 31:35.
“Their waves roar like many waters; the uproar (שְׁאוֹן) of their voice is given.”
“Let its waters roar and foam” (Hebrew numbering; English 46:3).
“Nations roared (הָמוּ גוֹיִם), kingdoms tottered”: three verses after the waters, the same verb of the nations (English 46:6).
“Your enemies roar, and those who hate you have lifted the head” (English 83:2).

“On the earth distress of nations in perplexity, sea and surge roaring (ἠχούσης θαλάσσης καὶ σάλου)”: the Greek verb that renders הָמָה in Isa 51:15, with the nations and the sea side by side as in Isa 17:12.

senses.definition: The low sound of a dog or a bear, the moaning of doves, and the sound of a harp or flutes to which a mourner's heart is likened.

evidence.note: “They return at evening, they growl like the dog (יֶהֱמוּ כַכָּלֶב), and go round the city”; again in 59:15 (English 59:6, 14).
“We growl like the bears, all of us, and like the doves we moan and moan (הָגֹה נֶהְגֶּה)”: set beside הָגָה.
The survivors on the mountains “like doves of the valleys, all of them moaning, each in his iniquity”.
“My inward parts sound like the harp (כַּכִּנּוֹר יֶהֱמוּ) for Moab.”
“My heart sounds for Moab like the flutes (כַּחֲלִלִים יֶהֱמֶה)”: the flutes of mourning.

senses.definition: Of a city and its streets full of people, of a loud and restless woman, of strong drink and those who have drunk: to be full of noise and stir.

evidence.note: Joab hears the horn: “Why is the sound of the city in commotion (קוֹל הַקִּרְיָה הוֹמָה)?”
“Full of shoutings, a city in commotion (עִיר הוֹמִיָּה), an exultant town.”
Wisdom calls “at the head of the noisy places (הֹמִיּוֹת)”, at the openings of the gates: the crowded streets.
“She is loud (הֹמִיָּה) and stubborn; her feet do not stay in her house.”
“The woman of folly is loud (הֹמִיָּה).”
“Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler (הֹמֶה שֵׁכָר).”
“They shall drink and be noisy as with wine (וְשָׁתוּ הָמוּ כְּמוֹ יָיִן).”
“Surely as a shadow a man walks about; surely for a breath they are in commotion (אַךְ הֶבֶל יֶהֱמָיוּן); he heaps up and does not know who will gather” (English 39:6).

senses.definition: Of the soul or heart of someone in trouble: to moan, to be in unrest within him. The psalmist answers it with “wait for God”.

evidence.note: “Why are you bowed down, my soul, and why do you moan within me (וַתֶּהֱמִי עָלָי)? Wait for God”; the refrain again in 42:12 and 43:5 (English 42:5, 11).
“My heart is in tumult within me (הֹמֶה לִּי לִבִּי), I cannot keep silence, for you have heard, my soul, the sound of the horn”: set against keeping silent (לֹא אַחֲרִישׁ).
“Evening and morning and noon I complain and moan (אָשִׂיחָה וְאֶהֱמֶה), and he hears my voice” (English 55:17).
“I remember God and moan (וְאֶהֱמָיָה); I complain, and my spirit faints” (English 77:3).
“Now is my soul troubled (τετάρακται)”: Jesus speaks of his soul as Psa 42:6 does, with the Greek verb whose compound renders תֶּהֱמִי in the refrain.

senses.gloss: be stirred with love or pity
senses.definition: Of the inward parts (מֵעִים): to be stirred toward someone, in compassion or in love. Yahweh says it of himself toward Ephraim.

evidence.note: “Is Ephraim my dear son? ... therefore my inward parts are stirred for him (הָמוּ מֵעַי לוֹ); I will surely have compassion on him (רַחֵם אֲרַחֲמֶנּוּ), says Yahweh”: the stirring is explained by the compassion that follows.
“My beloved put in his hand by the hole, and my inward parts were stirred for him (וּמֵעַי הָמוּ עָלָיו).”
For Moab: “my inward parts sound like the harp”, pity for a people under judgment.

evidence.locator: Isa.51.15, וַיֶּהֱמוּ → ἠχῶν (lemma ἠχέω); forms of the same verb at 1Ki.1.41, Psa.46.4, Isa.16.11, Jer.5.22, Jer.50.42, Jer.51.55 (the vendored file writes these with ξ for χ and leaves them unlemmatised)

evidence.note: “Sea and surge roaring (ἠχούσης)”, with the distress of nations.
“Sounding brass (χαλκὸς ἠχῶν)”: the sound of an instrument, as הָמָה of harp and flutes.

evidence.locator: Psa.46.7, הָמוּ → lemma ταράσσω; Psa.42.12 and Psa.43.5, תֶּהֱמִי → συνταράσσεις (the compound)

evidence.note: “Now is my soul troubled (τετάρακται).”
“Let not your heart be troubled.”

parallels.note: “Be in uproar”, with its noun שָׁאוֹן: the nearest word, of waters and of peoples alike.

evidence.note: יֶהֱמָיוּן and יִשָּׁאוּן in the two halves of the verse.
וְהָמוּ גַלֵּיהֶם beside שְׁאוֹן קוֹלָם.

parallels.note: “Moan, mutter”: of doves beside the growling of bears.
“Complain, muse aloud”: joined to it in prayer.
“Foam, be in ferment”: of the waters.

evidence.note: יֶהֱמוּ יֶחְמְרוּ מֵימָיו.

opposites.note: Hiphil “keep silence”: what the heart in tumult cannot do.

evidence.note: הֹמֶה לִּי לִבִּי לֹא אַחֲרִישׁ.

phrases.gloss: a city in commotion, a bustling city

evidence.note: הַקִּרְיָה הוֹמָה.

words.summary: The verb's noun in ־וֹן: first the sound (of rain, waves, wheels, songs, a crowd), then the commotion that makes it, then the crowd itself, above all an army or a people in its numbers, and so a great quantity of anything. About 85 uses: the count of 95 includes nine tokens of the name גּוֹג, counted here by a fault in the database's keys, and הֲמָנְכֶם in Ezk 5:7, which may be a verb. A third of them are Ezekiel's, of Egypt's multitude and of Gog's.

senses.definition: A loud, continuous sound: heavy rain, the waters above, waves, chariot wheels, many songs, the voices of a crowd. Often after קוֹל, “the sound of a הָמוֹן”.

evidence.note: Elijah to Ahab, before any cloud is seen: “for there is the sound of the roar of the rain (קוֹל הֲמוֹן הַגָּשֶׁם)”.
“At the sound of his giving, a roar of waters in the heavens (הֲמוֹן מַיִם בַּשָּׁמַיִם)”; the same in Jer 51:16.
“The sea has come up over Babylon; with the roar of its waves (בַּהֲמוֹן גַּלָּיו) she is covered.”
“At the rushing of his chariots, the rumble of his wheels (הֲמוֹן גַּלְגִּלָּיו).”
“Take away from me the noise of your songs (הֲמוֹן שִׁרֶיךָ), and the melody of your harps I will not hear.”
“I will make the noise of your songs cease, and the sound of your lyres shall be heard no more.”
“The sound of a הָמוֹן on the mountains, the likeness of a great people; the sound of an uproar of kingdoms”: the noise of an army mustering.
“The sound of his words was like the sound of a multitude (כְּקוֹל הָמוֹן).”
The lion “is not dismayed at their voice, nor cowed at their noise (וּמֵהֲמוֹנָם)”: the shepherds' shouting, beside קוֹל.
“As the voice of a great multitude (ὄχλου πολλοῦ), and as the voice of many waters”: John hears what Daniel heard (Dan 10:6), the crowd and the waters named together.

senses.definition: The noisy stir of many people: an outcry in a city, the confusion of a camp or a battle, the unrest of peoples.

evidence.note: Eli hears the city cry out: “What is the sound of this tumult (קוֹל הֶהָמוֹן הַזֶּה)?”
“The tumult that was in the camp of the Philistines went on and grew.”
Ahimaaz: “I saw the great tumult ... but I did not know what it was.”
God “stills the uproar of the seas, the uproar of their waves, and the tumult of the peoples (וַהֲמוֹן לְאֻמִּים)” (English 65:7).
“At the sound of tumult peoples fled.”
The wild ass “laughs at the tumult of the city (לַהֲמוֹן קִרְיָה)”.
“The palace is forsaken, the tumult of the city (הֲמוֹן עִיר) deserted.”
“Truly in vain from the hills, the tumult on the mountains”: the noisy worship of the high places, against salvation in Yahweh.

senses.definition: A great number of people together: most often an army with its following, also a people, a crowd at a feast, the population of a land or city.

evidence.note: Of the Aramean army: “Have you seen all this great multitude (הֶהָמוֹן הַגָּדוֹל הַזֶּה)? I am giving it into your hand today.”
“There is no strength in us before this great multitude that is coming against us”; “the battle is not yours but God's” (20:15).
“Sisera ... and his chariots and his multitude (הֲמוֹנוֹ).”
Asa: “in your name we have come against this multitude” (English 14:11).
“Do not be afraid of the king of Assyria and all the multitude with him, for with us is a greater than with him.”
The king of the north “shall set up a great multitude, and the multitude shall be given into his hand”; so 11:10, 12, 13.
“The multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel shall be as a dream, a vision of the night.”
“Multitudes, multitudes (הֲמוֹנִים הֲמוֹנִים) in the valley of decision”: the only plural beside Ezk 32:20 (English Joel 3:14).
David gave “to all the people, to all the multitude of Israel, man and woman alike”: set beside כָּל הָעָם.
“With the voice of joy and thanksgiving, a multitude keeping the feast (הָמוֹן חוֹגֵג)” (English 42:4).
“Its glory are men of hunger, and its multitude parched with thirst”: the nobles and the common crowd.
“By the swords of the mighty I will make your multitude fall”: Egypt's, as throughout Ezk 30–32.
“There they shall bury Gog and all his multitude.”

senses.definition: In Yahweh's covenant with Abram: the many nations he is to be father of, the phrase by which the name Abraham is explained.

evidence.note: “You shall be father of a multitude of nations (לְאַב הֲמוֹן גּוֹיִם).”
“Your name shall be Abraham, for father of a multitude of nations I have made you.”
Quoted: “father of many nations (πατέρα πολλῶν ἐθνῶν) I have made you”; the Peshitta, ܐܒܐ ܠܣܘܓܐܐ ܕܥܡܡܐ, “father to a multitude of peoples”. So הֲמוֹן here is number, “many”.
“That he might become father of many nations, according to what was spoken, So shall your seed be.”

senses.definition: A great quantity of things: goods, offerings, cattle, wives. In this sense it is set against “a little”.

evidence.note: “Better the little (מְעַט) of the righteous than the abundance (מֵהֲמוֹן) of many wicked.”
“He who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver, nor he who loves abundance (בֶּהָמוֹן) with increase” (English 5:10).
David, of the gold and silver for the house: “all this abundance that we have prepared ... is from your hand.”
Of the heaps of the contribution: “what is left is this abundance.”
“The abundance of the sea (הֲמוֹן יָם) shall be turned to you, the wealth of nations (חֵיל גּוֹיִם) shall come to you.”
“The multitude of their cattle a spoil.”
Rehoboam “sought a multitude of wives”.

senses.definition: Once, of Yahweh: the stirring of his inward parts, his compassion, as the verb in Jer 31:20.

evidence.note: “Where are your zeal and your mighty acts? The stirring of your inward parts and your compassions (הֲמוֹן מֵעֶיךָ וְרַחֲמֶיךָ) are held back from me”: paired with רַחֲמִים.

evidence.locator: Gen.17.4, הֲמוֹן → πλήθους (πλῆθος); Jdg.4.7; 2Sa.18.29; 2Ch.20.2, 12, 24; Isa.17.12; Jer.49.32; Ezk.30.10; Ezk.39.11; πλῆθος renders הָמוֹן ×23, its commonest rendering

evidence.note: From one man, and him as good as dead, were born “as the stars of the heaven in multitude (τῷ πλήθει)”: the promise to Abraham that Gen 17:4 puts as “a multitude of nations”.
“The multitude came together”: a crowd in a city.
Gen 17:5 quoted in these words.
“The waters which you saw ... are peoples and multitudes (ὄχλοι) and nations and tongues.”
“The voice of a great multitude, as the voice of many waters.”
“A great multitude which no one could number, out of every nation.”

evidence.locator: Jer.51.16, Jer.51.42 and 1Sa.14.19, הָמוֹן → lemma ἦχος

evidence.note: “The sound of a trumpet (σάλπιγγος ἤχῳ)”: a loud sound.
“A sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind.”

parallels.note: “Uproar”: its twin, of seas and of peoples.

evidence.note: הֲמוֹנָהּ וּשְׁאוֹנָהּ go down together.

parallels.note: “Voice, sound”: beside it, and before it in קוֹל הָמוֹן.
“Force, army; wealth”: beside it in both its senses.

evidence.note: “All his multitude ... Pharaoh and all his army (חֵילוֹ).”
הֲמוֹן יָם beside חֵיל גּוֹיִם.

parallels.note: “People”: the multitude is the whole people.

evidence.note: קוֹל הָמוֹן ... דְּמוּת עַם רָב.

parallels.note: “Glory”: the honoured men beside the common crowd.

evidence.note: “The glory of Moab shall be despised, with all the great multitude.”
The great multitude, and then “a remnant, a very little (מְעַט מִזְעָר)”.

opposites.note: “No strength”: those who face the multitude.

phrases.gloss: the sound of a roar, of a tumult, of a multitude
father of a multitude of nations
this great multitude (an army too strong to face)

evidence.note: הֶהָמוֹן הָרָב הַזֶּה.
“Pharaoh shall see them and be comforted over all his multitude (עַל כָּל הֲמוֹנוֹ).”
The name given to the valley in Israel where Gog and all his multitude are buried.
“And also the name of a city is Hamonah (הֲמוֹנָה)”: named from the same word.

phrases.gloss: the stirring of your inward parts

words.summary: Used once, so its sense rests on that verse and on the verb, which is said of the harp in Isa 16:11.

senses.definition: The sound of stringed instruments, which goes down to the grave with the king of Babylon's pride.

evidence.note: “Brought down to the grave is your pride, the sound of your lyres (הֶמְיַת נְבָלֶיךָ); under you the maggot is spread, and the worm is your covering.”

words.summary: The Peshitta's New Testament has the root ܗܡܐ only in this verb, three times, and not in the Hebrew's sense of sound or tumult: where the Greek has “roar” or “crowd” the Peshitta uses other words (ܩܠܐ ܕܝܡܐ, “the sound of the sea”, Luk 21:25; ܟܢܫܐ, “crowd”, Rev 17:15). How “neglect” goes back to the root is not clear, and no cognate has been found that ties it to the Hebrew: it is kept here by its spelling.

senses.definition: To let a thing pass without care for it.

evidence.note: “And Gallio disregarded these things (ܡܗܡܐ ܗܘܐ ܒܗܠܝܢ)”; the Greek, “none of these things was a care to Gallio”.
“My son, do not neglect (ܠܐ ܬܗܡܐ) the chastening of the Lord”, quoting Pro 3:11, where the Hebrew is אַל תִּמְאָס, “do not reject”.

senses.definition: To leave a thing undone on purpose.

evidence.note: “But I forbear (ܡܗܡܐ ܐܢܐ), that I may not seem to be frightening you by my letters.”

cognates.note: The Aramaic of the Targums has the same verb, used where the Hebrew has הָמָה of the heart (Jer 4:19) and of the waves (Jer 5:22): the two ends of the Hebrew's range, the sea's roar and inward unrest, in the one Aramaic word.

evidence.note: to be excited, to roar, rumble: Targ. Jer. 4:19; 5:22.

cognates.note: In the Targums at Isa 13:4 and 2Ki 25:11, verses where the Hebrew itself has הָמוֹן, so it may be the Hebrew word carried over and not an independent Aramaic noun.

evidence.note: multitude: Targ. Is. 13:4; Targ. II Kings 25:11.

cognates.note: A doubled root h-m-h-m, of a low continuous sound, as הָמָה of doves and bears. It imitates the sound, so the likeness may be no more than that; Lane's lexicon has no article on it.

evidence.locator: Arabic همهمة (hamhama), noun, root ه م ه م
evidence.note: verbal noun of هَمْهَمَ (form Iq); humming.

doctrine.statement: When Abram was ninety-nine and had no son by Sarah, Yahweh said, “you shall be father of a multitude of nations (אַב הֲמוֹן גּוֹיִם)”, and changed his name to Abraham, “for father of a multitude of nations I have made you” (Gen 17:4–5): spoken as done, before it was. Nations and kings were to come from him and from Sarah (Gen 17:6, 16). Paul quotes the verse and says who the multitude is: the promise is sure “to all the seed, not to that only which is of the law, but to that also which is of the faith of Abraham, who is father of us all, as it is written, Father of many nations I have made you”, before God “who makes the dead alive and calls the things that are not as though they were” (Rom 4:16–17); and Abraham “against hope believed in hope, that he might become father of many nations” (Rom 4:18). So also “those who are of faith, these are sons of Abraham”, the scripture having foreseen that God would justify the nations by faith (Gal 3:7–8), and “if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's seed, and heirs according to promise” (Gal 3:29). John sees “a great multitude which no one could number, out of every nation and tribes and peoples and tongues” standing before the throne (Rev 7:9). From the verses: the multitude of nations promised to Abraham is not only the peoples descended from him, but those of every nation who believe as he did and are Christ's; God named him their father while he was childless, as he calls things that are not as though they were.

The prophets use this root of the sea and of the nations in the same breath. “Woe to the tumult of many peoples, who roar like the roaring of seas ... nations rush like the rushing of many waters; but he rebukes it, and it flees far off”, and by morning it is gone (Isa 17:12–14). In Psalm 46 the waters roar and foam (46:4) and then “nations roared, kingdoms tottered; he gave his voice, the earth melted” (46:7). The army from the north has a voice that “roars like the sea” (Jer 6:23), and Babylon's fall is “the sea has come up over Babylon; with the roar of its waves she is covered” (Jer 51:42), though it was the nations' armies that came. John is told the meaning outright: “the waters which you saw ... are peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues” (Rev 17:15); and Jesus sets “distress of nations” beside “sea and surge roaring” (Luk 21:25). The same passages say who is over that sea. Yahweh set the sand as its bound, “and its waves roar and do not pass over” (Jer 5:22); he “stills the uproar of the seas, the uproar of their waves, and the tumult of the peoples” (Psa 65:8); he “makes wars cease to the end of the earth” and says, “Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth” (Psa 46:10–11). From the verses: in prophecy a roaring sea stands for nations and their armies in tumult, and its stilling for the end of their wars, when God is exalted in the earth.

The noise of the living stops at the grave. Of Jerusalem's revellers: “the grave has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without measure, and her splendour and her multitude and her uproar go down” (Isa 5:14). Of the king of Babylon: “brought down to the grave is your pride, the sound of your lyres; under you the maggot is spread, and the worm is your covering” (Isa 14:11). Ezekiel is told to wail over the multitude of Egypt and bring it down “to the land below, with those who go down to the pit” (Ezk 32:18); there Pharaoh and all his multitude lie among the slain, as Asshur and Elam and Meshech and Tubal lie, each with “her graves round about” (Ezk 32:22–26, 31–32). The multitude of Gog is buried in a valley in Israel, and the land is cleansed of their bones (Ezk 39:11–16). A man's stir while he lives is “for a breath” (Psa 39:7), and “the dead do not praise Yah, nor any who go down into silence” (Psa 115:17). From the verses: the grave to which the multitudes go down is where their bodies lie, with maggot and worm, among the buried; what goes down there with them is their sound, which ceases. Nothing in these passages has the dead still in tumult.

note: Drafted 2026-11-15. Root: המה, the key the database gives the verb and הָמוֹן (BDB e.bt.*); no existing entry had it. The id is `hamah`, not `hem`, because the pronoun is not here: BDB also files הֵמָּה “they” under this spelling (e.bs.aa, 565 tokens, with the cross-reference e.bz.ad), but hu.json already holds those keys with the Aramaic הִמּוֹ (xe.ah.aa) and אִנּוּן (xa.av.ab), as the plural of הוּא: a pronominal base with the plural ־ם, not a root (see hu.json's note). A key belongs to one entry, so nothing of the pronoun is repeated here; the summary points to it. Database: some הֵמָּה tokens carry word_info root המה (hu.json's note (e)), so their word sheet will now open this entry, which is wrong for them; fix in the lookup or by a surface override, not here. הִנֵּה, הֵן “behold” and הֵנָּה “hither” are in hinneh.json. Counts: e.bt.ab's 95 tokens include nine of גּוֹג (Ezk 38:2, 3, 16; 39:1 twice, 11 twice, 15; 1Ch 5:4), which the brief lists under this key by a fault (“also c.ay.ae”), and all its tokens are also matched to e.bv.ac (הָמַן) by spelling. Left out: (1) הֲמוֹנָה (e.bt.ad, Ezk 39:16), a city's name, and בַּעַל הָמוֹן (b.ci.ae, Sng 8:11), a place: places have no entries yet; Ezk 39:16 is cited under the phrase גֵּיא הֲמוֹן גּוֹג. (2) No personal name is formed from this root in the brief, so no name entry was written; אַבְרָהָם is explained by אַב הֲמוֹן גּוֹיִם in Gen 17:5 but BDB does not file the name here, and it is left to the entry of whichever root it is given. (3) הָמַן (e.bv.ac), to which Ezk 5:7 הֲמָנְכֶם is referred, and הָמַם, הוּם, נָהַם, הֲמֻלָּה (Ezk 1:24): neighbouring roots of like sound and sense, each its own spelling; Ezk 5:7 is counted among הָמוֹן's tokens but not cited. (4) מֶהֱמֵהֶם in Ezk 7:11 (“nor of their multitude, nor of their ...”), a word found only there beside מֵהֲמוֹנָם: it may be of this root, but it has no key in the database and its sense is not fixed by the verse; not entered. Sense notes: Jer 3:23 הָמוֹן הָרִים is taken as the tumult of worship on the mountains from the context (3:21–24), and Isa 32:14 הֲמוֹן עִיר as the city's bustle; both could be “multitude”. Psalm and Joel verses are in the Hebrew numbering (Psa 42:6 = English 42:5; Psa 46:4, 7 = 46:3, 6; Psa 65:8 = 65:7; Joel 4:14 = 3:14). Syriac: ܐܗܡܝ (SEDRA lexeme 800, root 509 HMA; neglect, cease, forbear) is entered by spelling with its three New Testament verses; the brief's Peshitta section found none because it looks for the key המה. Its tie to the Hebrew is unproven and it has no cognate named, so its balance in lexicon-support is negative. Leads not followed: Arabic هَمَى, said to mean “flow” and (of camels) “roam untended”, which could answer to the Syriac “neglect” and not to the Hebrew: Lane has no article همى (the letter ه is in his Supplement), only a remark in art. عمى that هَمَى means “it flowed”; Arabic هَمَّ “disquiet, make anxious” (Lane p. 3044) belongs with הָמַם. Wiktionary gives Classical Syriac ܗܡܢ (hāmān) “death; place of the dead” as borrowed from הָמוֹן, which would bear on Ezk 32 and 39:11; not verified in Payne Smith or Brockelmann, so not entered. Not consulted: CAD for an Akkadian cognate, DULAT for Ugaritic (hmlt “multitude” is of the root hml), Leslau for Ge'ez, CAL for the Aramaic verb outside the Targums. The Septuagint citations name lemmas and quote only forms the vendored lxx.tsv spells correctly: it writes ξ for χ in forms it has not lemmatised (ἠξήσει, ὄξλον), which is why the brief shows few lemmas for the verb.
